absaetze.t: Une fois jugés, pourront-ils enfin rentrer ? La question se pose pour les 47 Français qui comparaissaient depuis septembre en Irak pour appartenance à l'organisation État islamique. La France s'est toujours opposée au retour de ses ressortissants, mais aujourd'hui, le contexte pourrait avoir changé.
2 min Temps de lecture

Huit Français ont été condamnés à la prison à perpétuité jeudi 26 novembre en Irak, deux à 15 ans de réclusion et dix autres attendent toujours leur verdict. Lors de leurs audiences, la plupart ont plaidé coupable et tous ont exprimé des regrets d'avoir rejoint l'EI, certains demandant à être rapatriés en France.

Matthieu Bagard, l'avocat d'une grande partie de ces hommes, espère aujourd'hui pouvoir enfin accéder à leur requête : « Une fois que la peine devient définitive, il y a la possibilité de demander le transfert pour exécuter cette peine-là dans des prisons françaises. On l'a déjà fait pour les Français qui ont été condamnés en 2019, pour l'instant sans succès. Mais je crois que la situation a beaucoup évolué depuis et on a déjà saisi le Quai d'Orsay et le ministère de la Justice puisque c'est lui qui les traitera en priorité. »
Signature d'un protocole d'accord

Les autorités irakiennes ont notamment annoncé une rencontre dimanche dernier entre le ministre de la Justice irakien et l'ambassadeur de France à Bagdad au sujet de la signature d'un protocole d'accord portant sur le transfert de détenus condamnés. Un accord dans l'intérêt de l'Irak, pour qui ses prisonniers coûtent cher, mais aussi de la France.

« La France aurait un intérêt au retour de ces Français aussi parce qu'ils sont visés par des procédures ici et que les juges antiterroristes demandent leur retour. Ils ont émis des mandats d'arrêt les visant, ajoute Matthieu Bagard. Ces mandats sont entre les mains des autorités françaises : que nous les fassions exécuter, et maintenant que les Irakiens les ont jugés, que nous leur demandions également des comptes ici. »

Les associations de victimes de terrorisme en France appellent à leur rapatriement depuis des années pour qu'ils puissent être judiciarisés en France. Des organisations de défense des droits humains dénoncent également la précipitation des procès et un manque de respect des procédures légales.

items.titel: Treibstoffkrise in Malawi: Kaum Geld
items.anriss: Malawi leidet unter einer extremen Treibstoffkrise. Die fragile Wirtschaft hängt vom Tabakexport ab - zu schwachen Deviseneinnahmen kommt die Lage an der Straße von Hormus hinzu. Die Krise wirkt sich auf alle Lebensbereiche aus. Von C. …

absaetze.t: Malawi leidet unter einer extremen Treibstoffkrise. Die fragile Wirtschaft hängt vom Tabakexport ab - zu schwachen Deviseneinnahmen kommt die Lage an der Straße von Hormus hinzu. Die Krise wirkt sich auf alle Lebensbereiche aus.

Gerade hat Vincent Chingwalu etwas Benzin für das Motorrad, mit dem er seinen Lebensunterhalt als Motorradtaxifahrer in Lilongwe, der Hauptstadt von Malawi, verdient. Aber in den letzten Wochen verbringt er mehr Zeit damit, an Tankstellen auf Benzin zu warten als zu fahren.

Malawi steckt seit Monaten in einer Treibstoffkrise, wie sie selbst das krisengeschüttelte Land im Süden Afrikas noch nicht erlebt hat. Für Vincent Chingwalu heißt das: "Die Treibstoffknappheit beeinträchtigt mein Geschäft. Als es noch Benzin gab, konnte ich täglich mehrere Fahrten machen. Früher hatte ich zwölf oder 15 Fahrten pro Tag, heute nur noch drei oder vier."

Sein Einkommen hat sich dadurch halbiert. Die Familie hat kaum Möglichkeiten, das auszugleichen. Im Alltag ist das jeden Tag spürbar. "Die Preise für Einkäufe und Essen sind so gestiegen, dass ich mir die grundlegenden Dinge nicht mehr leisten kann. Dinge wie Waschmittel. Und wir lassen bestimmte Nahrungsmittel weg."

Durch den Treibstoffmangel ist auch das Gesundheitssystem Malawis massiv betroffen. Kliniken haben keine Reserven für ihre Notstromgeneratoren, Rettungsfahrzeuge sind nicht einsatzbereit. In mindestens einem Fall sind eine Mutter und ihr Neugeborenes gestorben, offenbar, weil es für den Rettungswagen, der sie in eine andere Klinik verlegen sollte, keinen Treibstoff gab.
Abhängigkeit von Tabakexporten

Malawi gehört zu den zehn ärmsten Ländern der Welt. Rund 70 Prozent der Menschen leben nach der Definition der Weltbank in extremer Armut. Das Land produziert nur wenige Güter, die es exportieren kann.

Dadurch kämen auch keine Devisen ins Land, um Treibstoff zu kaufen, sagt der Volkswirt Christian Franken von der Denkfabrik Oxford Economics Africa. "Im Kern geht es darum, dass die Wirtschaft Malawis kaum diversifiziert ist. Sie stützt sich weitgehend auf die Landwirtschaft, die etwa 20 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts ausmacht."

"Tabakexporte allein bestreiten rund 57 Prozent der gesamten Ausfuhren, weitere sieben Prozent entfallen auf Tee. Weil Tabak die wichtigste Devisenquelle darstellt, ist man von diesem einen Produkt abhängig, dessen jährliche Erträge außerdem stark schwanken", so Franken.

Die Devisenschwäche in Kombination mit den extrem hohen Ölpreisen aufgrund der Blockade der Straße von Hormus führen dazu, dass diese Treibstoffkrise extreme Ausmaße annimmt, und sie wirkt sich auf fast alle Wirtschaftszweige aus.

Eine ähnliche Krise im vergangenen Jahr führte dazu, dass sich die Lage auf dem sowieso schon prekären Arbeitsmarkt in Malawi weiter verschlechtert hat. Und auch wenn für dieses Jahr noch keine Zahlen vorliegen, dürfte die aktuelle Krise dazu führen, dass noch mehr Menschen ihre Jobs verlieren, sagt Franken.
Treibstoff landet auf dem Schwarzmarkt

"Ein weiteres Problem ist, dass ein großer Teil des Treibstoffs, der in Malawi ankommt, auf dem Schwarzmarkt landet", sagt der malawische Ökonom Wiston Katumbi. Viele Tankstellenbetreiber würden den Treibstoff horten, der dann zu noch höheren Preisen verkauft werde. Katumbi fordert zur Abschreckung harte Strafen.

Inzwischen hat die Regierung reagiert. Sie ruft die Bevölkerung auf, illegale Aktivitäten beim Treibstoffhandel zu melden. Konkret geht es um den illegalen Handel mit Benzin oder Diesel, das Umleiten von Lieferungen oder das unerlaubte Horten von Treibstoff in Lagern oder an Tankstellen. Denjenigen, die solche Fälle anzeigen, wird eine hohe Belohnung versprochen.

Aber selbst ohne den zusätzlichen Druck durch den Schwarzmarkt verteuerten sich gerade alle Produkte des täglichen Bedarfs, erklärt Wirtschaftswissenschaftler Katumbi: "Die Menschen können sich kaum noch Speiseöl oder Mehl leisten. Sie sind oft nicht einmal mehr in der Lage, ihre Kinder zur Schule zu fahren oder zur Arbeit zu pendeln."
Neue Regierung versprach bessere Wirtschaft

Die Schuld für die schlechte wirtschaftliche Lage geben viele der malawischen Regierung von Präsident Peter Mutarika, die das Land seit vergangenem Jahr regiert und die mit dem Versprechen angetreten war, die wirtschaftliche Lage zu verbessern.
Auch Ökonomen wie Franken sehen die Regierung in der Pflicht. Sie hätte schon längst die Landeswährung abwerten sollen, sagt er und rechnet mit diesem Schritt für das kommende Jahr.

"Trotzdem bleibt das grundlegende Problem bestehen: Die einzige Devisenquelle ist Tabak, ein Rohstoff aus einem schrumpfenden Wirtschaftszweig. Angesichts von El Niño und des Klimawandels ist diese Haupteinnahmequelle jetzt in Gefahr", so Franken.

"Eine Währungsabwertung allein würde hier kaum Abhilfe schaffen. Idealerweise müsste ein solcher Schritt unter der Aufsicht des IWF erfolgen, was die Glaubwürdigkeit der politischen Maßnahmen erheblich stärken würde." Die Landeswährung abzuwerten, dürfte also nur eine kurze Atempause für Malawi bedeuten.
Sprengung an einer neuen Mine für Seltene Erden in Malawi. Diese Rohstoffe könnten eine neue Einnahmequelle für das verarmte Land darstellen.
Mineralien und Tourismus als Optionen

Zumindest eine neue Einnahmequelle zeichnet sich gerade ab, sagt Franken: "In Malawi wurden Seltene Erden entdeckt. Es gibt schon Investitionen, und bald könnte die Förderung der Seltenen Erden beginnen. Das ist also eine Möglichkeit zur Diversifizierung." Man könne zwar auch versuchen, den Teeexport ausweiten, aber dabei handele es sich auch um für den Klimawandel anfällige Landwirtschaft.

Eine weitere Chance könnte es aber sein, mehr Touristen ins Land zu holen. "Malawi besitzt einen sehr bekannten großen See, den Malawi-See. Er erstreckt sich über einen beträchtlichen Teil des Landes. Hier gibt es vermutlich noch Spielraum, den Tourismus auszubauen. Es gibt also durchaus Optionen, aber es dürfte wohl noch eine Weile dauern, bis diese Alternativen das ausgleichen können, was der Tabaksektor derzeit für das Land leistet."

Kurzfristig bringen diese Ideen der Bevölkerung in Malawi keine Erleichterung. Für Menschen wie Motorradtaxifahrer Vincent Chingwalu ist die Treibstoffkrise schon jetzt zu einer existenzgefährdenden privaten Krise geworden. "Wenn die Treibstoffkrise weiter anhält, dann wird meine Zukunft schwierig", sagt er. Denn dann könne er sich die Miete für sein Haus und die Schulgebühren für seine Kinder einfach nicht mehr leisten.

absaetze.t: Im Golf von Oman hat das US-Militär nach eigenen Angaben ein Handelsschiff beschossen. Die Besatzung habe versucht, die US-Blockade iranischer Häfen zu durchbrechen. Das Schiff sei manövrierunfähig, die Crew unverletzt.
Das US-Militär hat nach eigenen Angaben im Golf von Oman ein Handelsschiff beschossen. Der Frachter habe trotz mehrfacher Warnungen versucht, die US-Seeblockade gegen iranische Häfen zu durchbrechen.

Das für US-Truppen im Nahen Osten zuständige Regionalkommando Centcom erklärte, dass das Schiff durch ein Militärflugzeug mit Präzisionsmunition am Heck getroffen worden sei. Dadurch sei der Antrieb lahmgelegt und das Schiff manövrierunfähig gemacht worden. Die Besatzung sei unverletzt.

Das Handelsschiff fuhr unter der Flagge von Palau, einem Inselstaat im Pazifischen Ozean. Kurz vor dem Beschuss sei es aus der iranischen Hafenstadt Bandar Abbas ausgelaufen. Schiffsverfolgungsportale nennen Singapur als Ziel des Frachters.

Das US-Militär setzt die Blockade iranischer Häfen dem Regionalkommando Centcom zufolge weiterhin "strikt" durch. Bislang seien sechs Schiffe manövrierunfähig gemacht und 158 weitere umgeleitet worden.
Häfen blockiert, Straße von Hormus dicht

Die USA hatten Mitte Juli nach dem Scheitern eines Abkommens mit Iran die Blockade iranischer Häfen verhängt. Iran hält seit Beginn des Iran-Kriegs durch Angriffe der USA und Israels Ende Februar die für den weltweiten Öl- und Gashandel zentrale Straße von Hormus weitgehend blockiert. In den vergangenen Wochen wurden dort fast täglich Angriffe auf Schiffe gemeldet.

Die diplomatischen Bemühungen um eine Beilegung des Kriegs stocken. Am Montag hatte das iranische Außenministerium angekündigt, alle dem Land zur Verfügung stehenden Mittel gegen die US-Blockade einzusetzen. Teheran erklärte, die Straße von Hormus könne binnen zwei Tagen wieder geöffnet werden, sofern Washington auf seine Forderungen eingehe. Dazu zählt die Aufhebung der US-Blockade.
Mit Informationen von Giselle Ucar, ARD New York

items.titel: Unique AIM-9X Sidewinders Now Seen On USAF F-35As In The Middle East
items.anriss: U.S. Air Force F-35A Joint Strike Fighters in the Middle East have started carrying AIM-9X Sidewinders painted almost entirely white or light gray. This is a scheme that does not appear to have been previously seen on these missiles. This, …

absaetze.t: U.S. Air Force F-35A Joint Strike Fighters in the Middle East have started carrying AIM-9X Sidewinders painted almost entirely white or light gray. This is a scheme that does not appear to have been previously seen on these missiles. This, in turn, could point to the emergence of a new version of the AIM-9X, and one specifically for the F-35 that might feature coatings to help reduce its radar cross section and/or other improved capabilities.

The Air Force has released pictures and video clips showing that its F-35As have been flying in the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility with the differently painted AIM-9Xs since at least November 3. At the time of writing, missiles with this scheme do not appear to have been spotted on any other U.S. aircraft type in the region or on Air Force F-35As operating elsewhere globally.

Since the AIM-9X first began entering service in the early 2000s, the standard paint scheme has been a dark gray nose section attached to a light gray main body. The missile’s tail fins have been painted in the same color as ones at the nose end.

On the AIM-9Xs recently spotted in the Middle East, only the very tip of the nose, which contains the seeker, is still darkly colored. The rest of the body, as well as the fins, have a uniform lighter color. In some pictures, the missiles appear to be largely white rather than gray, but this could just be a trick of the light. The video immediately below offers a close-up look at one of the missiles with what looks to be a very light gray coloring. The footage also appears to deliberately blur out certain markings on the missiles.
The reason for the change in coloring is unknown. TWZ has reached out to the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO) and Raytheon, the prime contractor for the AIM-9X, for more information.

The possibility has already been raised that what we are seeing is the newer Block II+ version of the AIM-9X, also known as the AIM-9X-3. The U.S. Navy, which is the lead service in charge of the Sidewinder program, has previously said this variant “incorporates specialized external materials to enhance aircraft platform survivability” and that it was specifically developed to “satisfy the requirements of the Joint Strike Fighter platform.”

The Block II+ version retained the improvements found on the preceding Block II AIM-9X-2 variant, which began entering service in 2015, including a lock-on-after-launch capability enabled by a new data-link. Compared to previous Sidewinder variants, the baseline AIM-9X had already been a major development, offering all-new high-off boresight targeting, thrust vectoring, and an advanced imaging infrared (IIR) seeker.

As TWZ has noted in the past, the AIM-9X-3’s “specialized external materials” could include new coatings and/or even structural changes to the baseline design to improve its stealthy characteristics. Developing a version of the AIM-9X with these features makes good sense in the context of the F-35. All versions of the Joint Strike Fighter are currently only able to carry AIM-9Xs externally under their wings, which negatively impacts the jet’s radar signature.

At the same time, the U.S. military ordered its first Block II+ AIM-9Xs in December 2017, and these missiles have been in inventory for years now. This raises the question of why we would only be seeing them in use now. New threat intelligence in the Middle East could have prompted the decision to use Block II+ rather than older AIM-9Xs. However, it has already been established that Iran, as well as the Houthi militants the regime in Tehran supports in Yemen, have air defense capabilities that can present risks to F-35s in certain circumstances.

Furthermore, in June, the Air Force released a picture of an F-35A flying in the Middle East carrying an AIM-9X with the standard paint scheme, but marked “F-35 USE ONLY.” This had also prompted discussions about whether the missile in question was a Block II+ version. At that time, TWZ had contacted the F-35 JPO to inquire about this marking and was directed to reach out to Warner Robins Air Force Base in Georgia instead.

A decision could have been made more recently to start painting Block II+ AIM-9Xs in a more distinctly different way compared to older versions for other reasons. Doing so could help make it easier for personnel on the ground to readily identify missiles intended for use only on F-35s. At the same time, this could indicate that the new paint scheme itself has no impact on signature. Though possible, this all seems unlikely due to known work done to provide new treatments to the missile to reduce vulnerability.

The paint job might also indicate a new variant or subvariant beyond the AIM-9X-3, including ones with further improved coatings of some kind applied. There are at least three other designated variants of the AIM-9X, though they all appear to still be in development.

The first of these is the System Improvement Plan III (SIP III) configuration, also known as the AIM-9X-4. This version includes hardware and software upgrades, including a new Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) processor.

“Integration of the ASIC processor into the AIM-9X-4 configuration has impacted missile reliability and halted testing,” according to an unclassified Modernized Selected Acquisition Report from the Pentagon, dated April 21, 2026. “Non-Ready-For-Issue (NRFI) AIM-9X-4 assets have negatively impacted Ao [operational availability] and Available Material (Am) rates. Recovery to the Ao requirement is anticipated to correlate to fielding of the AIM-9X-4 configuration in September 2027.”

There is also the AIM-9X-5, another SIP III version described as a direct companion to the -4 model, and the differences between the two are not immediately clear. Work is now underway on the further improved SIP IV configuration, or AIM-9X-6, as well.

A “Compact Variant,” or AIM-9X CV, is in development, but how much this missile will ultimately have in common with existing variants remains to be seen. Navy budget documents have described it as having a new “compact airframe optimized for internal carriage on advanced aircraft with improved kinematic performance.”

The long-term roadmap for the AIM-9X had previously included a more substantially evolved Block III version, which could have featured extended range and improved kinematic performance by using a new highly loaded grain rocket motor. The Block III plan was shelved, at least publicly, years ago, but the Navy has continued to invest heavily in this kind of rocket technology.

AIM-9Xs with new paint schemes might also reflect missiles in a subvariant configuration that has not received a separate designation. Such a version could have been developed in response to pressing needs in the Middle East, specifically, including optimization against particular target sets like longer-range one-way-attack drones. The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) think tank published a report last year saying that the Israeli Air Force (IAF) had modified older AIM-9M Sidewinders to be more effective against drones.
At that time we wrote:

“It isn’t clear what was modified, and if it was hardware or software based, or both, to increase its effectiveness against smaller, slower-flying targets, especially at lower altitudes, where various kinds of ‘clutter’ on the surface below can hamper detection and tracking. “Seeker” here could also be shorthand for a broader set of modifications to the Israeli AIM-9Ms. As something of a tangential example, years ago, the U.S. Army added new proximity fuzes featuring small conformal radar antennas to existing FIM-92 Stinger short-range, heat-seeking surface-to-air missiles to improve their effectiveness against various targets, and particularly drones.”

It’s also worth noting here that laser-guided 70mm Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II (APKWS II) rockets, originally designed as air-to-surface munitions, have become the Air Force’s go-to air-to-air weapon against drones. The Air Force, as well as other branches of the U.S. military, have been steadily integrating APKWS II onto a growing number of platforms for use in this role. However, F-35s are not able to employ the rockets at all currently.

Even optimized for the anti-air role, APKWS II also has major limitations, including the need for the target to be designated (or ‘lazed’) throughout the entire engagement. The rockets cannot aggressively maneuver, either, and therefore can only engage steady flying, non-reactionary, low-performance targets. The number of rapid engagements a fighter can execute in a given period is also limited due to the need to acquire and laser each target while getting into very close proximity of it so the rocket can reach. With all this in mind, Air Force F-16 fighters have been spotted in the Middle East in recent years carrying mixed loads of APKWS IIs, AIM-9Xs, and/or AIM-9Ms.

Older and newer Sidewinders are clearly still playing a major role in combat operations in the Middle East, in general. This was underscored just recently by the release of pictures showing a U.S. Marine Corps F/A-18D Hornet in the region loaded with AIM-9Ms and AIM-9Xs, as well as AIM-120 Advanced Medium Range Air-to-Air missiles (AMRAAM). Back in April, at the height of combat operations against Iran, our own Tyler Rogoway highlighted how valuable Marine F/A-18C/Ds with their new AN/APG-79(V)4 active electronically scanned array radars could be, particularly in the counter-drone role.

At this time, we cannot definitively say what the new paint job spotted on AIM-9Xs loaded on Air Force F-35As flying in the Middle East signifies. Still, signs now do point to the further evolution of an already very capable design.

items.titel: A cache of emails could never measure up to a stash of much-treasured letters
items.anriss: When was the last time that you wrote a letter? Picked up a pen and organised your thoughts on a piece of paper? Don’t worry – I am not going to come over all virtuous because I certainly can’t recall the last time that I folded a page of …

absaetze.t: When was the last time that you wrote a letter? Picked up a pen and organised your thoughts on a piece of paper? Don’t worry – I am not going to come over all virtuous because I certainly can’t recall the last time that I folded a page of vellum and popped it in an envelope. I still write thank-you notes and Christmas cards, though even here my commitment diminishes each year (when nonagenarians are now sending you Santa emojis instead of glittery cards adorned with plump robins, you might as well give in). But letters. Nah.

Last Saturday my friend Emily invited me and a whole gang of her mates to attend an event at London’s Royal Albert Hall, that vast rotunda of an auditorium perched beside Hyde Park. Some 5,000 people had rocked up for an event called Letters Live where, apart from a few musical interludes, all that happens is that starry actors come on stage to read a letter. Some of these are bawdy, others heartbreaking, wise, splittingly ferocious or just funny. There were letters that were centuries old, others written weeks ago. Will Sharpe, Benedict Cumberbatch, Himesh Patel, Suzy Eddie Izzard, Sharon Horgan, Aimee Lou Wood – it was a dazzling cast of readers.

But it was the letters that were the true delight. René Magritte telling critic Richard Dupierreux where he can stick his opinions – he refers to him as a “shit pump”, a phrase that I have stored for future use. Colette suggesting to her estranged husband that he should return to her embrace and stop seeing other women (even if Colette would not break from her female lover). A tabloid newspaper editor, Nick Appleyard, informing his staff about when swear words could and could not appear in a headline and the correct way to write bellend (“who the hell puts a hyphen in bellend!”).

But sitting there nursing my pint of wine – Emily knows how to spoil a boy – I couldn’t help but wonder what the people in the audience, enthralled by these literary trinkets, would leave behind for future generations to sift through? Emails Live doesn’t have quite the same ring to it, let alone Emojis Live. Now it’s not that people don’t write cracking memos – indeed Appleyard’s was an internal staff email – it’s just that how will anyone ever bloody find them if they don’t go viral in the moment?

While some great contemporary authors and artists will have diligent assistants archiving their emails, I imagine that most don’t. And even if they do bequeath their papers to a university library, will they also remember to hand over their email log-in? The password for their phone so that their emojis can be preserved and picked over?

When my mum died, several years after my dad had already shunted off, we had to sift and sort a series of boxes and tins that contained the things that they had never been able to let go of. A distillation of what they had treasured. There was the i-Spy book of birds and a tiny watch that had belonged to my brother, who had died in an accident. And letters.

In one of the tins, I found a letter that I had sent to them when I was 21. I had graduated from university, got on to a management-trainee scheme, had found an OK apartment but it didn’t feel good. I must have been cautious of phoning them – or perhaps I just wanted to set out my decision uninterrupted – but I wrote a letter telling them of my news. I wanted to have one proper go at becoming a journalist. I had resigned from my job and was picking up shifts in a bar. I remember that I left some time. A week? But when I finally called, all they had for me was love and their backing. And then one of them placed my letter in a tin. A marker of a moment, a change in direction.

There’s no going back. We are where we are. But let’s not pretend that something hasn’t been lost. A time when friendships, love affairs and battles could be revisited years later with a sharp immediacy. A time when the tangled courses of relationships were traced with ink on paper. A time when what was precious could be put in a tin at the back of a wardrobe. There, whenever needed. Waiting to be found many years later.

items.titel: Ahead of Taiwan local elections, politicians crowd in at Art Taipei
items.anriss: 127 galleries took part in the fair at Taipei World Trade Center

absaetze.t: This year's edition of Taiwan's 34-year-old fair Art Taipei (29 October to 2 November) and its third concurrent Taipei Art Week (TAW) fell, serendipitously, just before the alleged spying scandal that emerged around Taiwan's celebrated native son, the naturalised American Nvidia mogul Jensen Huang. This spared fair sales the ensuing worldwide tech stock dive. Rather, concerns during the fair focused more on the pending midterm elections on 28 November.

The fair's opening ceremony was thick with politicians. Prominent figures included incumbent Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, now in a close re-election race, who would days later face protests at the Taipei Pride parade and festival over his police department's aggressive raid of gay bar Commander D on 3 October. Taiwan's minister of culture Li Yuan heralded his department's successful efforts in September to get a pavilion at the Gwangju Biennale named for Taiwan rather than the sponsoring institution, which sparked a diplomatic row with mainland China, and pronounced that "AI will not replace artists!"

"The presence of political figures at art fairs is a familiar feature of Taiwan's cultural landscape," says Claudia Chen, director of Art Taipei, chair of its organiser, the Taipei Art Gallery Association (Taga), and cofounder of Taipei's Liang Gallery. She adds that it builds public visibility and engagement for the cultural sector. "We hope this attention can help deepen public understanding of the art market and highlight its close connections with cultural development, urban growth, and international exchange."

The question, she continues, "is whether this engagement with political leaders can translate into consistent policy support, particularly in areas such as arts education, international promotion, and incentives for private collecting and cultural patronage." Taiwan lags behind most East Asian governments in cultural investment. "We hope cultural development can become an important public issue and receive sustained support across political parties, allowing Taiwan to gradually translate its economic strength into a deeper and more far-reaching cultural influence."

Chen says that Taiwan's technology sector and the private wealth it fuels "provide an important foundation for its art market. However, translating economic growth into greater activity in the art market takes time," as well as innovation and outreach by galleries.

The 127 galleries that Art Taipei welcomed to the Taipei World Trade Center this year included the return of influential galleries such as Richard Koh Fine Art, from Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, for the first time post-pandemic, and Perrotin for a third consecutive year. Newcomers included Tokyo's Misako & Rosen. One of Taipei's leading platforms, Tina Keng Gallery (TKG+) and TKG+ Projects, joined for the first time in about five years. "In recent years, with Singapore, Seoul, Hong Kong, there is a lot happening, so we needed an opportunity to do a Taiwan show," says the gallery's assistant to the director, Alice Liang. With the suspension of the sleeker international fair Taipei Dangdai after 2025, Art Taipei has resumed its status as the main "hometown" option, she says.

Sales of a "museum-type" installation of works by artists including Sanyu, Kuo Tzumin and Michael Lin went "pretty well", says Liang. "People were surprised and curious," with "positive feedback" from collectors who skewed young and were both Taiwanese and foreign. She adds that the launch of the broader art week had little impact on sales, "but we can feel the difference, with the events, parties and open studios."

Fair organisers also report a generational shift among buyers, with 20.8% of those surveyed saying they were attending for the first or second time, double the figure for 2023. VIP collectors also declined from 77.5% to 54.2%, suggesting that the publicly accessible side of the art week is also providing outreach for the fair. Endeavours included five bus rounds, guided tours, digital art screenings at Taipei Lumitree and 30 public artworks displayed citywide, says Chen. For the art industry, a forum included speakers such as M+ Hong Kong curator Russell Storer and 2026 Venice Biennale Korea Pavilion curator Binna Choi.

The fair also featured an expanded presence of galleries from Korea and Japan, with 25 and 22 respectively, drawing on Taga's ongoing collaboration with those countries' gallery associations. Galleries from Japan, Taiwan's former coloniser, "have maintained a longstanding presence in the Taiwanese market, with many having established strong collector networks and brand recognition over the years," says Chen. The Korean presence "demonstrates the Korean art industry's capacity to expand into international markets through collaboration."

Tastes at the fair are also shifting towards Pop and contemporary art, says dealer Steven Chen (no relation). His Taipei gallery Yiyun Art has attended the fair for seven of the past ten years. It represents traditional Asian paintings, which remain a major sector at Art Taipei, if reduced from previous years. His dramatic maze of a booth, evoking a Chinese scholar's garden, saw steady crowds and sales, including of a painting by Yu Cheng Yao for $90,000. "With the young generation is coming more to the fair," says Chen, "we need a new language on ink art. It is the same culture with a new expression."

Claudia Chen says that Taiwan's collectors are maintaining "purchasing momentum" but have become increasingly deliberate, needing time and established relationships with galleries. Meanwhile, younger collectors are "gradually entering the market, bringing more diverse perspectives shaped by their own lifestyles and aesthetic preferences."

items.titel: Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow
items.anriss: Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.

absaetze.t: Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.
According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa.
Programa’s Schedules function acts as a streamlined alternative to spreadsheets, detailing each item’s code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.
The extension runs inside SketchUp and allows designers to link components in the model to matching products in the Schedule.
As a result, designers can track an item from the first 3D sketch through to its final specification, without entering the same information separately in SketchUp and Programa.
From the model, designers can send a component to a chosen Schedule, or link it to a product that is already listed there.
Programa explained that linking to an existing product creates a connection without adding a duplicate line item, keeping the Schedule “clean” as the design is fleshed out.
Before anything is added, designers can review and edit the product’s information.
The Schedule entry combines the details available from the component with anything entered during that review.
Programa said this gives studios a chance to check the specification before it is used for pricing or procurement.
The extension also provides access to Programa’s Product Library within SketchUp.
Designers can place saved 3D models directly into their designs, and use product images as material swatches to bring selected finishes into the model.
In this way, the products (and finishes) a studio has chosen can be seen in the visuals as well as listed in the Schedule.
The process also works in reverse, starting from the Schedule. A product with a compatible 3D model attached can be placed straight into SketchUp.
If there is no model, designers can choose a stand-in from SketchUp’s 3D Warehouse, or from elsewhere in the current model, to represent the product.
Once a component and a product are connected, supported changes can be reviewed and applied in either direction.
For example, adding another copy of a connected chair in SketchUp generates a quantity change, which the designer can then apply to the Schedule.
The company added that changes are presented for review “before the corresponding update is applied”.
This means the model and the specification can move together as a design develops, while the Schedule is only updated once the designer has chosen to apply a change.
Programa stressed that responsibility remains with the studio.
Designers stay in charge of “selecting the right product, checking its details and deciding when the model or Schedule should change”, the company said.
The aim, it explained, is to carry information between the model and the specification rather than make those decisions on the designer’s behalf.
The extension is aimed at studios that model in SketchUp and manage their specifications in Programa.
The Programa extension works with SketchUp desktop on Mac and Windows.
To learn more, visit Programa’s website or its extension setup guide.

items.titel: Notes from the underground: Why you should dig deep to find your people
items.anriss: The underground carpark is alive with the sound of music ( writes Blake Matich ). Yodelling, to be specific. Herders and farmers have long used the Alpine practice to talk shop across valleys of old and pastures new. But in Graz, Austria, …

absaetze.t: Culture
November 27, 2026
3 Min Read
There’s more than vocal flips and falsettos to be found in the depths of a subterranean yodelling class. Far below the mainstream, you might just find something more profound: your tribe.

The underground carpark is alive with the sound of music (writes Blake Matich). Yodelling, to be specific. Herders and farmers have long used the Alpine practice to talk shop across valleys of old and pastures new. But in Graz, Austria, where the relatively flat surroundings of the Grazerfeld plain are not as echo-friendly as hills and mountains, a group of some 30 yodellers have found an acoustic alternative – and friendship, presumably – in the subterranean Kastner & Öhler parking garage.

Yodelling isn’t the first thing that comes to mind when you think of underground scenes, literal or metaphorical. In my twenties, going “underground” meant partying in a former public toilet beneath a Berlin intersection or dodging stalactites rum-drunk as I descended into La Cueva, a cavernous club within a Cuban hillside. No sooner had I sunk to the nadir of this discoteca in a natural cave and double-parked myself with a fresh pair of cuba libres than I noticed a woman sat on a table, draped in snakes, surrounded by four scantily-clad dancers who proceeded to lift said table using only their mouths (a corner each). You know, the kind of good, clean, cave-dwelling hijinks that you hope to find in the nether regions.

But now that I’m making good progress in my thirties, it’s nice to know that there are scenes that aren’t a bog-standard toilet rave or a snake cave. These days, I make more modest descents and following the sound of the underground usually finds me improvising comedic riffs in the basement of a King’s Cross church or sipping mocktails in the sort of Bertie Wooster-style speakeasies that always seem a police whistle away from being raided by truncheon-wielding bobbies. Anyone fancy a piña no-lada at The Jaundiced Newt?
Still, it’s nice to know that, despite an increasingly homogenised world, exploring underground and alternative scenes is still a bona fide way to find your people – even if they’re yodellers.

Some scenes don’t even necessitate a dip below the surface. In Japan, the lure of the underground meets cultural restraint in the form of “manholers”. Get your head out of the gutter – we’re talking about a community of enthusiasts for the creatively illustrated manhole covers that put a colourful lid on the country’s sewer system. If you’re looking for a weird niche, Japan has you covered.

Even just finding a good book club can be an ordeal. Some are so underground that they don’t even exist. A Vanity Fair investigation by Clara Molot published this week exposed the International Institute of Literature & Arts (IILA), a prestigious society of literature scholars. The esteemed professors listed among its fellows should have known better than to judge a book by its cover. The IILA is, in all likelihood, a Chinese intelligence op. When asked to comment on the IILA, a Chinese embassy spokesman said: “I am not familiar with the specific situation that you mentioned.” Translated from diplomacy talk, this means: The first rule of the International Institute of Literature & Arts is that you do not talk about the International Institute of Literature & Arts.

International conspiracies aside, the modern world seems intent on housing us in silos. Thankfully we’re free to dig tunnels between them. Can’t find the club, class or community that fits the bill? Never fear – there’s no shortage of niches and crannies underground. Whether you’re yearning to yodel or want to join the ranks of the academic literati for the small price of a membership fee and eternal fealty to the Chinese Communist Party, there’s an underground scene for you. Your people are out there. You might just have to dig deep to find them.
